en: The End of the Story of Śrī Rāma. Now begins the Bālakāṇḍa.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Śrī, whose chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa,
I shall relate the account of Śrī Rāma as proclaimed by the venerable Vālmīki.
In former times, there was a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa who was the son of Viśravas;
he had two younger brothers, Kumbhakarṇa and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having brought the Creator face to face through intense asceticism,
they chose their desired boons from him who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge in him.
Rāvaṇa chose invincibility against anyone other than humans, and likewise his younger brother Kumbhakarṇa,
desiring the state of being godless, chose sleep.
Vibhīṣaṇa, endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva), chose devotion to Viṣṇu;
having granted these boons to them, the Lord vanished right there.
Then Rāvaṇa, having gone there and defeated the Lord of Wealth in battle,
seized the city of Laṅkā and the Puṣpaka chariot, and dwelt there in happiness.
Then all those Yātudhānas, dwelling in the subterranean realm (rasātala),
took refuge with the Ten-faced one and lived happily in Laṅkā.
Having married Mandodarī, the daughter of Maya,
the Ten-faced One begot upon her a son named Meghanāda.
Having conquered the world of the nāgas and the subterranean realm of Rasātala, that Rāvaṇa assailed all the worlds and carried off beautiful women.
Corrupting Vedic rites, he oppressed the twice-born;
accompanied by his son, he also tormented Vāsava in battle.
Having had those jewel-trees brought back again by his servants and having established them in Laṅkā, he dwelt there for a long time.
Then, at that moment, the inhabitants of heaven approached the Creator and reported all of Rāvaṇa’s activities.
Having heard that, the Creator, together with the gods, reached the shore of the Ocean of Milk and praised Hṛṣīkeśa with various hymns.
Then the enemy of the Daityas, having appeared, questioned the Grandfather:
"For what purpose have you come here together with the hosts of gods?"
Then Aja reported his suffering caused by the Ten-faced one;
having heard that, Viṣṭaraśravas spoke to the Creator, gladdening him.
"Enough with fear, O self-born one; go together with the hosts of gods.
Having become the son of Daśaratha, I shall slay the ten-faced Rāvaṇa."
And may all the gods, through portions of themselves, be born on earth in the form of monkeys to assist me in the subjugation of Rāvaṇa.
Having spoken thus to the Creator, the Lord vanished on the spot;
but the Lotus-born One, his mind filled with joy, departed together with the gods.
From him, Śakra begot the monkey named Vālin;
Mārtāṇḍa begot Sugrīva, and Māruta begot Hanumān.
Long ago, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] produced Jāmbavān;
in this manner, other gods as well produced many monkeys.
Then Vālin became the sovereign of the hosts of monkeys,
and together with all these [monkeys], he dwelt in Kiṣkindhā.
Now, there was a king named Daśaratha in the solar dynasty;
although he obtained three wives, he did not obtain offspring through them.
Then, following the words of Sumantra, that king, together with his family priest, brought Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and began the sacrifice for the desire of a son.
Then, someone rising from the fire took a vessel of milk-rice porridge and,
saying "Eat this, you are the wife," he offered it to the king.
Having taken that, he, full of longing, had his wives eat it at that very moment;
and from eating it, they conceived embryos from the king.
Then, when the time was fulfilled, Kausalyā gave birth to Rāmacandra, the sun to the lotuses of virtuous people, and likewise Kaikeyī gave birth to Bharata.
Then Sumitrā gave birth to two sons, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna;
their father had the brahmins perform for them the birth rites and other ceremonies.
Then those four, being affectionate toward one another, grew in stature and attained proficiency in all branches of knowledge.
Then, on one occasion, the great sage Viśvāmitra arrived and requested the assistance of Rāma— who was like the wielder of the Śakti spear— for the protection of his sacrifice.
At the word of Vasiṣṭha, the king, with great reluctance, placed Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, into the hand of that Kauśika.
Taking them with him as he departed, he likewise instructed Bala and Atibala in all the weapons.
As he proceeded with his younger brother, the wise Rāma, urged on by Kauśika,
slew Tāṭakā, who was intent upon afflicting the world.
Then, having reached Siddhāśrama together with Rāghava, Kauśika commenced the sacrifice, and the Rākṣasas gathered there.
Then Rāghava, having cast Mārīca into the ocean with a divine weapon and having slain Subāhu and his followers, protected the sacrifice of the sage, O Sage.
Then, being led by Kauśika along with his younger brother, Rāma—
having brought about Ahalyā’s release from the curse— reached the city of Maithila.
Honored by Janaka and urged by Kauśika,
Rāma broke the divine bow that had been brought for the sake of Sītā.
Then the Lord of Mithilā, having summoned Daśaratha by means of messengers,
gave his daughters, Sītā and the others, to his sons, Rāma and the rest.
Then, having performed the marriage by the command of his guru,
Rāghava, together with his younger brother, set forth, highly honored by Janaka.
Having heard of that breaking of the bow, which was terrifying due to his wrath,
Rāghava returned to Ayodhyā after defeating Paraśurāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then, bringing joy to all people through his own deeds,
the descendant of Kakutstha dwelt there happily together with Sītā.
Thus ends the Bālakāṇḍa in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa.
Now begins the Ayodhyākāṇḍa.
In the meantime, Bharata, accompanied by Śatrughna, joyfully set out for the house of his maternal uncle Yudhājit.
Then, having consulted with his ministers together with the subjects, that king,
filled with joy, began the consecration of Rāma.
But Kaikeyī, her mind corrupted by Mantharā, requested from the protector of the earth the fulfillment of two boons previously granted, as he was bound by his promise of truth.
The lord of the earth granted her two boons with difficulty: for Rāma’s dwelling in the forest and for Bharata’s attainment of the kingdom.
At that very moment, Kaikeyī commanded Rāma to dwell in the forest;
having taken leave of all his elders, he set out for the woods.
Seeing that he had departed, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa followed him;
all the citizens, abandoning their own homes, also pursued him swiftly.
Having deceived those citizens while they slept at night, Rāghava ascended the chariot being driven by Sumantra and departed.
Then, having gone to Śṛṅgaverapura on the bank of the Gaṅgā, Rāghava,
honored there by Guha, stayed for one night.
Having summoned his charioteer, he, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
crossed the Jāhnavī by means of a boat brought by Guha.
Having approached the sage Bharadvāja and bowed to him, Rāghava was hospitably received by him; at his direction, he dwelt happily on Citrakūṭa.
Then, having gone to Ayodhyā overwhelmed with grief, Sumantra reported everything regarding Rāghava’s conduct to the king.
Having heard what was spoken by Sumantu, the king, his mind bewildered by grief, cried out "Rāma! Rāma! and, casting off his body, went to heaven.
But the ministers, having preserved the body of the king at the word of Vasiṣṭha,
quickly summoned Bharata from his maternal uncle’s residence by means of messengers.
But Bharata, having heard that his father had died because of Kaikeyī’s words, performed his funeral rites and other ceremonies according to the prescribed rules along with his younger brother.
Although urged by his ministers toward the kingship at that time, Bharata nevertheless departed for the forest with the citizens to bring Rāma back.
Having gone there, together with Vasiṣṭha and other brahmins, he entreated Rāma— who was staying at Citrakūṭa wearing bark garments and matted hair— to protect the kingdom.
"Having spent fourteen years, I shall return again to the city," saying this and giving him his sandals, Rāma sent him back with confidence.
Taking those sandals from him, Bharata, with a dejected mind,
remained in Nandigrāma and protected the earth by means of them.
Rāghava, having gone from that mountain, paid homage to Atri;
his wife, for her part, then adorned Sītā with her own ornaments.
Having stayed for one night in that hermitage, Rāghava,
accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
Thus ends the Ayodhyākāṇḍa in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa.
Now begins the Āraṇyakāṇḍa.
While traveling through the forest, the descendant of Kakutstha then slew Virādha, who— impelled by fate— was carrying away himself, his wife, and his younger brother.
Having reached the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and observed his ascent to heaven, he—
being entreated by the sages— vowed the destruction of the rākṣasas.
Therefore, having gone there and bowed down to Sutīkṣṇa, who honored him in return,
the best of the Raghus reached the hermitage of Agastya and paid his respects to him.
The pot-born sage Agastya bestowed upon Rāma the bow of Viṣṇu, a pair of quivers belonging to Indra,
the Brahmā-weapon, and a sword.
Then, as he was proceeding, that descendant of Kakutstha met Jaṭāyu;
he entrusted the protection of Vaidehī to him, who was as dear to his father as a son.
Then, having reached Pañcavaṭī, he dwelt happily there with Sītā in a leaf-hut constructed by Lakṣmaṇa.
Once, having approached Rāma there, Śūrpaṇakhā made a proposal;
rejected by him, she then proposed to Lakṣmaṇa, but he too rejected her.
Then, afflicted by desire, she chose Rāma, who resembled the god of love;
but being rebuked by him once more, she rushed toward Sītā in a rage.
Then, her ears and nose cut off by Lakṣmaṇa out of rage,
she went to Janasthāna and reported this to Khara.
Hearing that, Khara became enraged and set out to slay Rāghava,
accompanied by the Yātudhānas headed by Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras.
At that moment, having entrusted Sītā to Lakṣmaṇa, the joy of the Raghus,
possessed of no small prowess, slew Khara along with his followers in battle.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, having gone to Laṅkā filled with grief,
reported the entire account from the beginning to Rāvaṇa.
Having heard that, Rāvaṇa then resolved to abduct Sītā;
reaching Mārīca’s hermitage, he urged him to provide assistance.
He too, having become a golden deer, roamed before Sītā;
she, however, entreated her husband to capture that deer.
Having appointed Lakṣmaṇa to protect Sītā, the joy of the Raghus quickly pursued the deer as it fled into the depths of the forest.
And Rāma, having assumed his own form, pierced the deer;
then, crying out "Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!", he gave up his life.
Having heard this from Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, being earnestly urged by her,
prayed to the deities for her protection and went into the presence of Rāghava.
In the meantime, Rāvaṇa, assuming the form of an ascetic, approached her,
seized Sītā, and departed through the sky filled with joy.
Then Jaṭāyu, beholding Jānakī being carried away,
attacked Rāvaṇa and struck him violently with his beak, wings, and claws.
Having severed him with his sword Candrahāsa and cast him down upon the ground,
Rāvaṇa took Sītā and entered his own palace.
Having stationed Janaka’s daughter in the midst of the Aśoka grove,
Rāvaṇa appointed night-stalkers to guard her.
Having slain Mārīca, Rāma returned;
hearing the news brought by his younger brother, he was overcome with grief and approached the leaf-hut.
Not finding Vaidehī there, while searching within the depths of the forest, he,
along with his younger brother, beheld the king of the vultures with its wings severed.
Having heard the news of Janaki spoken by him, and having subsequently cremated him who was dead,
Rama, together with his younger brother, performed the water-libation rites for him.
Seeing her subsequently attempting to overpower him on the road, Lakṣmaṇa quickly turned Ayomukhī into one whose ears and nose were severed.
Those two arms, seized by Kabandha, he lopped off;
then, entreated by him, they caused his body to be cast away.
Having assumed a divine form, he said to Rāma, "Go to Sugrīva, who is staying on Mount Ṛṣyamūka, for the sake of finding Sītā," and then he departed for heaven.
Then, pleased, the best of the Raghus went to Śabarī’s hermitage;
honored by her, he subsequently reached Lake Pampā together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Thus ends the Āraṇyakāṇḍa in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa.
Now begins the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa.
Then Hanumān, directed by Sugrīva, having reached and learned the circumstances regarding Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, united them with him.
Then, having reported the news of Rāma to Sugrīva,
he caused a friendship to be established between the two of them in the presence of the sacred fire.
Then Rāma vowed, "I shall slay Vālin," and he promised another thing, saying,
"I shall show you Vaidehī."
Then Sugrīva informed Rāma of the cause of his enmity with his brother, as well as the entirety of that brother's superior strength.
At that moment, Sugrīva displayed Dundubhi’s body,
which Rāghava sent far away with his big toe.
Furthermore, O best of the Raghus, he cut down seven palm trees that had been pointed out by him with a single arrow, out of apprehension for his safety.
Having reached Kiṣkindhā together with Rāma, Sugrīva then roared most exultantly, inciting the lord of the monkeys to anger.
Vālin emerged and tormented Sugrīva severely in the encounter;
with all his limbs shattered, he too fled to the presence of Rāghava.
Having been marked with a sign by Rāma, he again swiftly challenged Vālin to battle; meanwhile, Rāma remained there, concealed from view.
Then Vālī, wearing a golden garland, having rejected the beneficial advice spoken by Tārā,
became enraged and engaged in a most dreadful battle with his brother.
Having pierced Vālī with an arrow, Rāma felled him to the ground;
and he too, recognizing [the shooter] as Rāma, abandoned his body and went to heaven.
Afterward, the best of the Raghus, who is compassionate toward those who seek his protection, consoled Sugrīva as he was grieving and made him the lord of the monkeys.
Then, on the ridge of Mount Mālyavat, Rāma, joined by Lakṣmaṇa and grieving for his separation from Sītā, dwelt there for four months.
Then, at the command of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa brought the lord of the monkeys,
together with the forest-dwellers headed by Hanumān, to the mountain.
Upon seeing Rāghava, Sugrīva, following his instructions, dispatched the monkeys to search for Sītā in all four directions.
Then Rāma placed the ring upon Hanumān’s hand;
taking it as a token of trust for Vaidehī, he departed.
Then the monkeys, led by Hanumān, having gone toward the southern direction and searching for Sītā, reached the Vindhya mountain.
Due to the transgression of their agreement, they undertook a fast unto death there;
and there they heard the news concerning Sītā, which had been proclaimed by Sampāti.
Then the monkeys, headed by Aṅgada, reached the ocean;
yet none among them was capable of leaping across it.
Then, emboldened by those words of Jāmbavān which praised his own prowess,
the son of the Wind ascended Mount Mahendra.
Thus ends the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa.
Now begins the Sundarakāṇḍa.
Then, having paid homage to all the immortals, the son of the Wind leaped from that mountain in order to cross the ocean.
Having leaped over Maināka and paid homage to Surasā,
and having slain Siṃhikā through his skillful policy, he reached the far shore of the great ocean.
Having conquered the presiding deity of Laṅkā and entered it,
the son of the Wind searched for Sītā and beheld Rāvaṇa sleeping at night.
Not finding Vaidehī there, he searched here and there;
having gone to the Aśoka grove, he saw a certain woman in distress.
Having climbed a certain tree and being well-concealed by its foliage, the son of the Wind sat there, speculating that "this must be Sītā."
Then Rāvaṇa, afflicted by passion, approached Maithilī and entreated her in many ways, saying, "Become my wife."
"I shall not be subject to your power," she rejected him;
then Rāvaṇa, his soul overcome by lust and anger, departed.
When Rāvaṇa had departed, that son of the Wind-god spoke to the lamenting Sītā,
related the news of Rāma, and gave her his signet ring.
Taking that up and lamenting again most bitterly, Vaidehī gave the crest-jewel into his hand, and he took it.
"Do not despair, O Queen; Rāghava will slay Rāvaṇa in battle and lead you away. Having thus comforted her, he departed.
That wise man, having reflected, destroyed that grove and slew many demons, such as Akṣa and others, in battle.
Then, having been captured in battle by Śakrajit,
the son of the Wind-god reported the prowess of the Lord of the Raghus to Rāvaṇa.
With his tail set ablaze by the rākṣasa,
he, having completely burned Laṅkā and crossed the ocean, returned to the monkeys.
Having gone together with the monkeys and reported everything he had done to Rāghava, he presented that crest-jewel as well.
Thus ends the Sundarakāṇḍa in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa.
Now begins the Yuddhakāṇḍa.
Then, together with countless hosts of monkeys led by Sugrīva,
Rāghava set out swiftly and reached the shore of the great ocean.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, abandoned by his brother, approached Rāma;
Rāma, the crusher of enemies, consecrated him in the sovereignty of Laṅkā.
Having been granted a path by the ocean, he had a bridge constructed there by Nala;
having traveled across it, he reached Mount Suvela.
Then, commanded by Rāghava, the foremost monkeys led by Nīla,
with trees and rocks in their hands, besieged Laṅkā from all sides.
Having slain the rākṣasas led by Prahasta who had emerged for battle at the command of Rāvaṇa, those heroes, possessing the prowess of lions, let out a roar.
Sugrīva, Hanumān, as well as Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa—
possessing terrifying prowess— slew many Rākṣasas in battle.
Then the son of Rāvaṇa, having approached in battle, bound Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with a serpent-noose; Garuḍa, the enemy of serpents, liberated them both.
Then Rāvaṇa, having been defeated in battle by the descendant of Raghu,
quickly awakened Kumbhakarṇa and dispatched him to slay Rāma.
Having gone forth with the rākṣasas, that descendant of Raghu swiftly slew Kumbhakarṇa along with his followers as he was devouring the monkeys.
Furthermore, Indrajit, skilled in the use of weapons, once again bewildered the best of the Raghus along with his younger brother and the monkeys in battle by means of the Brahmā-weapon.
At that very moment, Hanumān went and brought the mountain of medicinal herbs;
having quickly awakened them all, he established it in its proper place.
Then, having gone to Nikumbhilā, the son of Sumitrā, together with Vibhīṣaṇa,
prevented Indrajit from performing his sacrifice and slew him in battle.
Hearing that, the enraged Rāvaṇa went forth and, having afflicted the monkeys with showers of arrows,
fought fiercely with Rāma.
Rāma also, having engaged in a most terrible battle with him for a very long time,
slew that enemy— who had received a boon from Brahmā— with the Brahmāstra.
Then Śakra and the other gods, rejoicing at the subjugation of Rāvaṇa,
showered a rain of flowers upon the head of the best of the Raghus.
Having appointed Vibhīṣaṇa as the lord of the rākṣasas,
Rāma accepted Maithilī, who had been purified by entering the fire.
Having quickly restored the monkeys to life by means of the boon of Purandara,
that best of the Raghus gratified them with various stores of wealth.
Then, having ascended the Puṣpaka chariot together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāma set forth along with the monkeys and the lord of the Rākṣasas.
While returning toward Ayodhyā, having sent the son of the Wind-god and ascertained Bharata’s intention, he arrived at Nandigrāma.
Having met with his brothers and cast off his ascetic garb,
Rāma entered Ayodhyā together with his joyful kinsmen.
Then Vasiṣṭha, together with the twice-born, in the presence of the ministers and vassals,
consecrated Rāma along with Sītā according to the prescribed rites.
Delighting the entire world like the moon on a full-moon night,
Rāma dwelt for a long time in Ayodhyā together with Sītā.
Then, as the night-stalker was devouring the hosts of monkeys,
Rāma also struck him violently in battle with the Aindra weapon.
Then Devāntaka and Narāntaka, dispatched by Rāvaṇa,
were slain at the forefront of the battle by Hanumān and Aṅgada.
Then Lakṣmaṇa struck with his arrows the massive-bodied Atikāya, who was advancing on a chariot and afflicting the army.
Then, commanded by Rāvaṇa, Śakrajit bound the two descendants of Raghu with the Brahmāstra in battle and slaughtered the monkeys with his arrows.
Then, having gone to the Mountain of Herbs at the word of Jāmbavān,
the son of the Wind-god, not seeing the medicinal herbs there, became enraged.
Having uprooted that mountain and returned with it,
he restored Rāghava and all the others to life by its fragrance.
Seeing the city burnt by the monkeys, Rāvaṇa, filled with rage,
dispatched the two sons of Kumbhakarṇa to slay the two descendants of Raghu.
Then, seeing those two powerful warriors afflicting that army,
Rāma slew Kumbha with his arrows, and the son of the Sun (Kumāra) slew Nikumbha.
Then Rāghava struck with a divine weapon the son of Khara, who had been incited by that Rāvaṇa and was afflicting the monkeys with his arrows.
Then, with a burning heart, Rāvaṇa urged his son, who was fierce in battle, to slay the two descendants of Raghu in combat.
Indrajit, the victor in battle, quickly departed from the city after having dispatched the illusory Sītā for the purpose of deluding everyone.
While the monkeys, headed by Hanumān, were looking on,
the victor in battle struck Sītā with his sharp sword.
Then, abandoning the battle and surrounded by all the monkeys,
the sorrowful Hanumān went quickly to where Rāma was.
Then Hanumān approached Rāma and told him everything;
having heard the entire account, Rāma fell into a state of fainting.

Then Vibhīṣaṇa, having arrived and seeing that Rāma was unconscious, spoke these words to comfort the dejected monkeys: "Vibhīṣaṇa, then, having arrived and seeing that Rāma was unconscious, spoke this while consoling the despondent monkeys with his voice."
O Lord, Leader of the World, abandon this false despondency;
having understood the mind of Rāvaṇa’s son, listen to the words I have spoken.
Indeed, an illusion was created by that evil-souled son of the lord of the Rākṣasas;
it is said that he has now performed a sacrifice at Nikumbhilā.
Send Lakṣmaṇa this very day along with me and the ministers;
once the oblation has been performed there, the enemy will certainly become invincible.
Rāma said to the son of Sumitrā, "Go quickly with your friend, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, and slay the son of the lord of the rākṣasas."
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having taken leave of Rāma, together with Vibhīṣaṇa,
quickly reached Nikumbhilā, where Indrajit was staying.
The righteous Vibhīṣaṇa introduced his brother’s son;
Lakṣmaṇa then began to pierce the Rākṣasas with volleys of arrows.
Having fought there for a long time with the Aindra weapon in great wrath,
the son of Sumitrā indeed severed the head of the son of Daśānana.
Hearing of his son’s slaughter, Rāvaṇa, emaciated by grief,
his fortitude lost, his limbs agitated, and his senses distraught, lamented.
My birth has been in vain, and my speech has been in vain,
since today I behold Indrajit slain in battle.
"Where have you gone, O hero, slain by a mere human foot-soldier—
a wretched man fallen from his kingdom— who has abandoned me, his son, and his own life?"
Having conquered Indra and bound him by force, you brought him to Laṅkā and,
through your prowess, made him a prisoner in a dungeon.
Brahmā released you after consoling you, O Lord of the Immortals;
where have you gone today, so difficult to approach, having abandoned me?
"What shall I do, my son? Where shall I go? Tell me now! Lead me wherever you are going; let there be no delay for you."
"There is no one equal to you in the worlds; I am the father of such a one"—it was with this intention that I remained here, O son, out of pride.
Dhūmrākṣa, Vajradaṃṣṭra, and the powerful Kumbhakarṇa—
all these Rākṣasas were slain, as were all those headed by Prahasta.
But disregarding all those Rākṣasas, even though they had struck out,
your son, O son, remains standing comfortably, relying upon his own strength.
Having lamented thus in many ways there, Rāvaṇa suppressed his inner sorrows and gave way to a most terrible rage.
"O charioteer, prepare my chariot quickly for me who am desirous of victory;
I shall go forth from my palace to slay Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa."
Having said this, he mounted the chariot quickly prepared by his charioteer;
then, having encountered Rāma, he engaged in a most terrible battle.
Then, having ascended the chariot of Indra brought by Mātali,
the righteous-souled Rāma shone like the sun situated at its rising.
While the host of gods looked on,
Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, waged a tumultuous battle out of the anger born from the abduction of Sītā.
Then, at the word of Agastya, the illustrious Rāma slew Rāvaṇa, the thorn of the worlds,
in battle with the Brahmā weapon.
Having heard of the death of her husband, who was most dear to her,
Mandodarī went to the battlefield and lamented, being deeply distressed like an osprey.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, commanded by Rāma, together with the rākṣasas,
performed the cremation of that Rāvaṇa whose life had departed.
Then, having seen Sītā as utterly pure by the word of Agni and being authorized by the hosts of gods, Rāma accepted her in the presence of his father.
This deed, which strikes fear into all the worlds, is indeed fitting for you alone;
therefore, O Rāma, it was done for the sake of Vaidehī, yet she is Lakṣmī herself and you are her own source of being.
Thus honored by the hosts of gods and by the sages,
Lakṣmaṇa rejoiced, and Rāma attained confidence.
The righteous, truth-abiding, and noble-minded Vibhīṣaṇa,
endowed with fortune, caused his own consecration to be performed by his younger brother.
Then, having ascended the Puṣpaka chariot together with his friends, the Lord of the World,
Rāghava, reached Kiṣkindhā accompanied by his wife and younger brother.
All the beloved wives of the monkeys dwelling in Kiṣkindhā,
out of curiosity for Sītā, ascended the aerial chariot Puṣpaka.
Then the illustrious son of Daśaratha, desiring to see Bharata,
arrived at the hermitage of Bharadvāja and was stopped there by him.
Rāma sent Māruti to the presence of Bharata,
who, due to not seeing Rāma, was intensely longing to enter the fire.
There, that lord of sages, overcome with joy, then honored Rāma along with his younger brother and his circle of friends according to the prescribed rites.
Then Rāma, having united with Bharata, the slayer of enemies,
quickly entered Ayodhyā, being greeted with joy by his mothers.
Then all those people dwelling in Ayodhyā, being thoroughly gratified,
approached Rāma and quickly said, "We are blessed!"
Just as cātakas upon seeing clouds and peahens upon finding their young find satisfaction, so too did the people on earth attain joy.
Then Vasiṣṭha and the others, filled with joy, together with the ministers, performed the consecration of Rāma, just as the Vasus did for Vāsava.
At the consecration festival, all the lords of the monkeys, headed by Sugrīva,
were honored as was fitting with garlands, perfumes, garments, and ornaments.
Hanumān received even greater joy from being honored by Sītā with a pearl necklace than he had felt upon the sight of her.
And Kausalyā, who was devoted to her son, adorned all the female monkeys with ornaments, garments, sandalwood, and saffron.
Then, by the command of Rāma, all the monkeys, Sugrīva and the others,
who were distressed by their separation from Śrī Rāma, reached Kiṣkindhā with great difficulty.
Devoted, long-lived, and the one who brought about the conquest of Laṅkā,
Vibhīṣaṇa, having been granted permission by Rāma, departed for Laṅkā.
Having obtained his father’s throne together with his brothers, the sinless Rāma shone forth just as Viṣṇu does in heaven.
With Lakṣmaṇa’s consent, Rāma bestowed the position of crown prince upon the immeasurable Bharata, who was dearer to him than his own life.
Those four great-souled ones, the best of the Raghus, together with their wives,
shone in their own city like the moon among the stars in the sky.
Thus ends the Yuddhakāṇḍa in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa.
Now begins the Uttarakāṇḍa.
"The king indeed accepted his wife even though she had been defiled by Rāvaṇa"—
by such talk of ignorant people, Rāma abandoned the princess of Mithilā.
Having learned of this, Vālmīki then brought her to his own hermitage;
having comforted her as she was pregnant, he settled her there in comfort.
Then, at the command of Rāghava, who had been entreated by the sages,
Śatrughna slew Lavaṇa in battle and protected them.
Then, having slain a Śūdra named Śambūka who was performing austerities, the best of the Raghus restored the dead son of a certain Brahmin to life.
While Rāma was performing a sacrifice, having fashioned a golden image of his wife,
the son of Pracetas brought Sītā along with her sons and gave her to him.
Furthermore, being thus suspected by Rāma, the daughter of Janaka entered the chasm that had been offered by the Earth when she was entreated [for refuge].
Lakṣmaṇa, having been overlooked by Rāma due to a lapse caused by fear,
cast off his human body and entered his own original form.
Then, at the command of Rāma, the forest-dwellers, together with the citizens,
bathed in the sacred ford of the Sarayū, cast off their bodies, and ascended to heaven.
Then Bharata and Śatrughna regained their own forms,
and Rāma too, casting off his human body, entered his own abode.
This account of the life of Śrī Rāma has been narrated by me, one of dull intellect;
let it be examined, corrected, and accepted by wise and virtuous men.
I perpetually bow to those gurus, who are devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, by whose grace the life-story of Rāma has been narrated by me.
But he who, having become the son of Daśaratha and having slain Rāvaṇa in battle,
protected the worlds as Vaikuṇṭha— may that one consisting of pure consciousness protect me.
Thus ends the Uttarakāṇḍa of the glorious Rāmāyaṇa.
The account of the illustrious Rāma is completed.
